title: Welcome to fairdatanow
text:
Effective interdisciplinary cooperation in data science projects requires smooth access to both data and code. And with the recent development of two amazing open source frameworks (self hosted Nextcloud for data storage and Jupyter notebooks for computing), we are now in a position to actually make this happen. Recently our lab (the Rijkserfgoedlaboratorium in Amsterdam) has installed a Nextcloud server that gives our lab the possibility to share data files organized in project folders with research partners. These can be accessed manually via a web interface, but also programmatically with the webdav protocol! With fairdatanow we want to learn how to easily find en download data files from a Nextcloud storage directly in Jupyter notebooks in order to explore them and create visualizations.
Under the hood the fairdatanow makes use of the Nextcloud Python Framework nc-py-api for communication with the cloud server, and the powerful holoviz Python packages and for creating interactive tables.
Although the package is still under construction it is already available for installation from the python package index.

title: An image processing example
text:
The holoviews way
Given these rather big files, we can use the awesome Python package holoviews to create an interactive visualization in a few lines of code in 15 seconds on my machine…

import imageio.v3 as iio
import holoviews as hv
from holoviews.operation.datashader import rasterize 
import panel as pn


hv.extension('bokeh')











  










  




  
  








ⓘ





pn.extension(sizing_mode='stretch_width')











  





# Read the 28 tif files into arrays 
ims = [iio.imread(im_file) for im_file in im_files] 

# Convert into holoviews images
hv_images = [hv.Image(im) for im in ims] 

# Rasterize to reduce size and speed up loading 
rasterized_ims = [rasterize(hv_im, width=500, height=500) for hv_im in hv_images] 

# Embed images in interactive viewer 
image_panes = [pn.pane.HoloViews(raster_im.opts(xaxis=None, yaxis=None, cmap='gray', tools=['hover'], title=titles[i])) for i, raster_im in enumerate(rasterized_ims)]


# Create a grid 
#xrays = pn.panel(pn.GridBox(*image_panes, ncols=6))

xrays = pn.GridBox(*image_panes, ncols=6)

xrays

title: Getting started with Python
text:
In order to make full use of fairdatanow you need to be able to install Python packages and run Python code in Jupyter notebooks on your computer. The quickest and easiest way to get started with Jupyter notebooks is by downloading and installing the JupyterLab Desktop (JLD) installer for your operating system from the official github repository.







Note



The first time you start JupyterLab Desktop you additionally need to install the default Python environment from the start menu. To do so you need to hoover and click on the word ‘install’ on the bottom of the start up screen.


Finally you can install or update (with the -U option) the fairdatanow package from the Python Package index pypi.org by executing this command in a Jupyterlab terminal:
pip install -U fairdatanow 
For more information about JupyterLab Desktop see the JLD user guide.
That is it! You now are ready to open up your explore (y)our Nextcloud data for your project.

title: Exploring your remote data in a breeze
text:
In order to to make use of fairdatanow, you will need a Nextcloud server url and credentials to access a folder on a (self hosted) Nextcloud server.
from fairdatanow import SaveLogin
To get started you need to import the DataViewer class from the package and instantiate it with the Nextcloud login() and **filters() functions. Depending on the amount of files in the cloud storage it might take some time to build the interactive file table. In this example we want to create a table for 8118 files (and counting) from the Falnama project which takes about 13 seconds.
from fairdatanow import DataViewer, login, filters
Given the complete overview of all data files in a project, you typically want find a subset of files for inspection further exploration. As an example let’s try to to filter the Infrared Reflectography (IRR) image tiles that were taken from page 71803-01 depicting the Moon. In most cases it would be sufficient to filter the file list with a simple search string search='Moon_IR tiles' in combination with a extensions=['.tif'] filter. However we see in this case that that we get a list with 73 files. So we need to be more specific. Additional filtering can be done with an advanced regular expression filter: search='.*Moon_IR tiles_\d', use_regex=True. The _\d part of the search pattern implies that after an underscore the filename should include at least one digit.
url = 'https://laboppad.nl/falnama-project' 
dv = DataViewer(login(url), **filters(search='.*Moon_IR tiles_\\d', use_regex=True, extensions=['.tif']))

Connection with nextcloud server is ok.
dv
link
Below the filtered file table one can see that we have selected exactly 36 files out of 8118 files in the Nextcloud storage.
We can now download these files into a cache folder on your local computer in order to process them further. This can be done easily with the .download_filtered() method.
files = dv.download_filtered()

title: Annotating your shared data with TOML
text:
If your research team starts to turn every stone very soon you will be facing a large pile of files. How to make sense as team of thousands of shared data files in your cloud storage with new uploads every week? In an ideal world we would all agree on a well defined folder structure. We would apply perfectly clear file naming conventions. And we would provide sufficient metadata with every file. All in order to help the colleagues in our team to make sense of the data collectively. In our heritage science lab with we do not have that luxury. As an interdisciplinary team working with primitive software applications, severely limited time budgets and high costs of artwork logistics it is difficult enough just get to get the measurements done and uploaded to the pile of files on our Nextcloud server. This is what I call the Missing Metadata Syndrome.
This implies that data sharing is not smooth at all. As a consequence data analysis is highly inefficient and it is hard to share insights that can be derived from the data within the team. In order to fix this problem we should stop dreaming about metadata magically appearing. Instead we should start to annotate our data. This means that we should discover and explore specific portions of the data to answer targeted questions and make annotations that help us to remember how to find back requisite data files.
The best way to do this is to store these annotations in simple text files that can be read both by humans and computers. The most suitable format for doing this is the so called TOML file format.
crumbs: Annotating your shared data with TOML

title: Annotating your shared data with TOML

Tom’s Obvious Minimal Language

import os

import holoviews as hv 
from holoviews import RGB, opts 
from holoviews.operation.datashader import rasterize
import panel as pn

toml_txt = '''
# On which locations within our ten World Museum Japanse prints did Gauthier and Tessa measure an XRF spectrum? 
# And what do these spectra show?  

# Measurements have been done on a selection of 10 prints that are present in our lab 
# here are the 10 object numbers of th prints located in Amsterdam

object_numbers = [
 'RV-1-4468-544',
 'RV-1-4469-484',
 'RV-1-4469-58',
 'RV-1-4469-x6',
 'RV-1-4469Q',
 'RV-1-4470-12',
 'RV-1-4470-27',
 'RV-360-2345g',
 'RV-360-2359-2',
 'RV-360-6886']


# The data table is linked to all search queries necessary for fairdatanow within this table are subtables that indicate the type of file the querie downloads.
# These subtables don't necessarily have to be file typing but can also be grouped by object. For this example we chose to use filetype to lessen the amount of branching at the top of the dictionary generated by the data_now function.
[data.spx]
# these are regexes that download all .spx files per object number  
RV-1-4468-544 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4468-544.*[.]spx"
RV-1-4469-484 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4469-484.*[.]spx"
RV-1-4469-58 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4469-58.*[.]spx"
RV-1-4469-x6 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4469-x6.*[.]spx"
RV-1-4469Q = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4469Q.*[.]spx"       # duplicate so no XRF spectra 
RV-1-4470-12 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4470-12.*[.]spx"
RV-1-4470-27 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4470-27.*[.]spx"
RV-360-2345g = ".*XRF.*RV-360-2345g.*[.]spx"
RV-360-2359-2 = ".*XRF.*RV-360-2359-2.*[.]spx"
RV-360-6886 = ".*XRF.*RV-360-6886.*[.]spx"

[data.jpg]
# these are regexes that download all .jpg files per object number  
RV-1-4468-544 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4468-544.*[.]jpg"
RV-1-4469-484 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4469-484.*[.]jpg"
RV-1-4469-58 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4469-58.*[.]jpg"
RV-1-4469-x6 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4469-x6.*[.]jpg"
RV-1-4469Q = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4469Q.*[.]jpg" # duplicate so no jpg's for point locations 
RV-1-4470-12 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4470-12.*[.]jpg"
RV-1-4470-27 = ".*XRF.*RV-1-4470-27.*[.]jpg"
RV-360-2345g = ".*XRF.*RV-360-2345g.*[.]jpg"
RV-360-2359-2 = ".*XRF.*RV-360-2359-2.*[.]jpg"
RV-360-6886 = ".*XRF.*RV-360-6886.*[.]jpg"

[data.tif] 
# these are regexes that download all .tif files per object number 
RV-1-4468-544 = ".*akama.*RV-1-4468-544[.]tif"
RV-1-4469-484 = ".*akama.*RV-1-4469-484[.]tif"
RV-1-4469-58 = ".*akama.*RV-1-4469-58[.]tif"
RV-1-4469-x6 = ".*akama.*RV-1-4469-x6[.]tif"
RV-1-4469Q = ".*akama.*RV-1-4469Q[.]tif"
RV-1-4470-12 = ".*akama.*RV-1-4470-12[.]tif"
RV-1-4470-27 = ".*akama.*1-4470-27[.]tif"      # TIF NAME WITHOUT RV prefix!  
RV-360-2345g = ".*akama.*RV-360-2345-?g[.]tif"
RV-360-2359-2 = ".*akama.*RV-360-2359-2[.]tif"
RV-360-6886 = ".*akama.*RV-360-6886[.]tif"

'''

Using the powerful data_now() function we can now download (or actually synchronize) all data files from the Nextcloud server that match the patterns in those tables in the toml file that start with [data.<some_key>] to the fairdatanow cache folder on our local computer. The progress of the download is indicated by a progress bar. The output of the function is a dictionary like object that contains file paths.

url = 'https://laboppad.nl/ukiyo-e-world'
data = data_now(url, toml_txt)
